sections.title: Step 1: identify your dominant defensive state
Step 3: normalize your dominant defensive state
Step 7: include realistic supports and encouragement

toc.title: Keep your narrative short and focused

blocks.p: Let's put the pieces together and purposefully craft a new self-narrative. (The ideas behind it are in [You're stuck, not broken](piece:stuck-not-broken).) We'll keep it general, focusing on your current state as a reflection of your past experiences. But we won't delve into your past experiences explicitly. (If you want to do so, don't let me stop you, but it's unnecessary for this part of your journey.) If you can't complete one of the steps, that's okay. Come back to it when you're ready.

blocks.h3: Step 1: identify your dominant defensive state

blocks.p: You're not broken or defective. You're stuck in a defensive state.
Example: My dominant state is shutdown.
Extend this further by adding a starting point as best you can. It doesn't need to be exact.
Example: I've been stuck in this state for around two years.

blocks.h3: Step 3: normalize your dominant defensive state

blocks.p: Does it make sense why you are in a stuck defensive state that began around that time? Don't go into details of the context, but recognize the general context.
Example: Based on the context of my life, it makes sense that I have existed in this state since then.
Yes, you've already had success. You're here. You're still going. And you got through whatever it was, or you're getting through whatever it is.
Example: I'm still here, and I've gotten this far.

Your defensive state isn't there for no reason. You got stuck due to life contexts. Your state kept you alive, even if it was difficult. It adapted to ensure you got your needs met. Give it some recognition and appreciation for getting you through it and to this moment.
Example: My state numbed me when I needed it and got me to this point.
You got stuck due to various life factors. Your stuckness is not your fault. However, your change is your responsibility. No one can do it for you.
Example: Now, I am ready for more self-regulation and safety in my body. It's time for a change, and I can make the next steps on my journey.

blocks.h3: Step 7: include realistic supports and encouragement

blocks.p: You're not on this journey alone. You have some sort of connection with others. They may not be obvious, but connections can be: spouses, partners, friends, professionals, support groups, religious, spiritual, and more.
Example: I'm not alone; my partner is a wonderful support.
Hope indicates that you have safety in your system and are on the right path. Wrap up your new narrative with a dash of hope about your future.
Example: I believe I can learn and implement the next steps.

blocks.prompt: Your turn. Write your own: your dominant state, a starting point, why it makes sense, your success so far, appreciation for your state, owning your change, your supports, and some hope.

blocks.p: Put it all together.

Example 1: My dominant state is shutdown. I've been stuck in this state for around two years. Based on the context of my life, it makes sense that I have existed in this state since then. I'm still here, and I've gotten this far. My state numbed me when I needed it and got me to this point. Now, I am ready for more self-regulation and safety in my body. It's time for a change, and I can make the next steps on my journey. I'm not alone; my partner is a wonderful support. I believe I can learn and implement the next steps.

Example 2: My dominant state is sympathetic fight. I've been stuck in fight since I was at least 11. Knowing what I know about my life, it totally makes sense why I have been stuck in fight since then. I'm still here; I have great kids and lots of hope for my future. My state helped me deal with a house that was dysregulated. But I am an adult and ready to feel more calm. I can do this. My Church is an incredible support, especially my pastor. I have no doubt I can learn and make a change for the better.

Example 3: Flight is my dominant state. I feel it constantly. I've been feeling anxious flight as far back as I can remember. I've consistently been in anxiety-producing and even dangerous circumstances. I've also struggled with finances a lot. So, it makes sense that I feel this way. I'm still going, though with no plans of stopping or giving up. My flight state has helped me deal with some genuinely stressful situations. If I wasn't always anxious, I probably would have given in and given up a long time ago. It's up to me and I have the power to do so. I'll also utilize the [Unstucking Academy](https://www.stucknotbroken.com/checkout/co-regulator) to get new ideas and connect with others. I know for damn sure I can do this and live with more calm in my body. I can't wait!

blocks.h: Keep your narrative short and focused

blocks.p: "That's it?!" you ask. "The narrative is that short?!"
"Yeah, that's it," I respond. "Short and sweet."
"What about my parents?! What about attachment? What about specific traumatic incidents?! What about the depths of my life and the pain I've been through?!"

Of course, all of those pieces are important. I'm not discounting, minimizing, or neglecting them as part of your trauma recovery journey. But we need to keep the focus on the present moment at this phase. More specifically, we focus on your knowledge and narrative in the present moment: nothing more and nothing less.

Other books, programs, and courses undoubtedly lead you in those directions. They encourage and walk you through how to process those pieces of who you are. They encourage you to explore the depths of your pains and suffering. They might even instruct you to write a narrative around what happened. Maybe even repeatedly.
But that's not what we're doing here.

We're focusing on the present moment. In the present moment, you may not have the safety capacity within you to delve into those depths. It's not necessarily helpful to take things further at this point. I think those other modalities fundamentally get this piece wrong or downright neglect it.

The point of creating a new narrative here is not to rehash old ones. Your new narrative respects the past and even appreciates the state you existed in to survive the past. But it focuses on the present moment and what is to come. For now, we acknowledge the past without getting sucked into it. We'll keep focusing on the present moment and what's to come. We always exist in the present moment. That is where we begin and where we end. The past affects you in the present. Your future is planned for in the present.

If you make your narrative too elaborate and far-reaching, there is a greater chance of getting pulled into past traumas and pains. You likely have layers upon layers of stuff floating around within you. It's never as simple as processing one event or relationship in isolation. There's always more to it. For example, if you attempt to involve your parents in your narrative, that will connect to other pieces from family, which will connect to cultural norms, which might connect to how that shows up in relationships, which will connect to self-worth, anger at yourself, and on and on. Let's not do that. Keeping things short and focused keeps you in the present moment and opens up the next step: building safety.

I listed some challenging aspects in the previous paragraph, but these didn't even include the specific trauma narratives. I've lost track of how many people have told me they entered into shutdown after detailing their past traumatic incidents. Certain therapeutic practices require you to do so (EMDR), even repeatedly (TF-CBT), or drudge up previously unknown traumatic incidents the client survived (brainspotting). This isn't me sharing an opinion. I am telling you what clients tell me. ("I think I just went numb and checked out to get through the narrative." "They waved this wand around and eventually got me to remember something, which just triggered me into dissociation. Then they sent me on my way, all dysregulated.") In an effort to cope with this overwhelm, the body understandably goes into shutdown. Retelling trauma narratives is not only unnecessary at this point but potentially harmful.

I hope you noticed some clarity and openness from learning the Polyvagal paradigm and creating a simple and short new narrative. Your efforts here hopefully provide some immediate top-down regulation, which opens up the potential for working on your safety state. It should reduce the cognitive load on your system.

As you keep working on getting unstuck, continually return to the short narrative. Returning to the narrative may be especially useful when you notice self-blame, shame, or judgment surfacing. Focus on the present, return to your narrative, and then continue with your practices and next steps.

You will find more safety in your system in the next phase, resulting in more calm and curiosity. Your interest in processing your past won't be there as it once has been. At least, that's been the experience of clients and [Unstucking Academy](https://www.stucknotbroken.com/checkout/co-regulator) students. As they build safety, they become more curious about their present-moment experiences, both external and internal. They want to know more about their underlying emotions and sensations, even the once-uncomfy ones, and how they connect with the past. Here, reflecting on the past will come from curiosity, not because one must do so. Curious reflection on the past is a result of self-regulation, not a necessary component leading to self-regulation. And yet, the reverse is the prevailing "wisdom" and expectation elsewhere.

We're taught that to heal trauma, one must delve into it. They must confront the past contexts that traumatized them. They must discuss in exquisite detail the events. And then do it again. And again. Until their practitioner tells them they are done or until they can tell the story without emotional upheaval. This approach focuses on the present and your capacity to stay connected to it. Once you are self-regulated enough, then you proceed into the stuck defensive state and whatever comes with it. But you do so lightly, at a pace you decide, when you decide.
"But Justin, I'm ready for that deep work! I want to feel all my stuff now! I want to reflect on my parents and my relationships. Let's do this!"

No, seriously. I don't recommend pushing into the past, especially if all of this is new to you. If you're just setting out, take your time. Work slowly. Even if you're a seasoned veteran in trauma work, I invite you to go slowly with me. You may find a brand new way of reflecting on your past without getting into the specifics of the details. I've worked with many people who have done lots of therapy, coaching, retreats, and more, who were dumbstruck by how simple and direct these concepts and techniques are. One of my therapy clients, training to become a Jungian therapist, reflected on how many times he painfully reflected on the past, doing "shadow work" for hours, uncovering the pains of childhood, and processing his dreams. He said, "I can't believe how simple this is. I've probably retraumatized myself many times over from my current practices."

Yes, it is possible to apply your new Polyvagal knowledge to specific moments in your life. You can apply the Polyvagal states to your experiences with romantic partners, friendships, parents, and more. You could apply your understanding of neuroception to a moment in your life when you froze. You could reflect on times you lacked co-regulation from others.

If you venture forth into more narrative work about the past through the lens of the Polyvagal paradigm, I implore you to approach these specific moments from your safety state. Approach them with curiosity and self-compassion. Waiting and approaching these narratives another time might be a good idea if you don't feel those.

I'm struggling to think of a client or course student who has intentionally reflected on past traumatic events or relationships in their self-regulation practices. We may do so in therapy as relevant and as they are ready. But outside of therapy, during their own practices? I can't think of anyone that purposefully spent time on past traumas. I don't think I have ever assigned that as homework to a client. It isn't part of my coursework. I don't recommend it to them or to you. I know, I'm repeating myself. It's that important.
